utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Good afternoon. As Judge Orie has pointed out the other day, when procedural matters were being discussed, he himself is absent today due to Tribunal business; and Judge Stole and I will continue on basis of Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Presiding Judge Orie himself will be back tomorrow and will be familiarised with today's transcript immediately after the hearing. The main content of today's hearing will be the testimony of retired Colonel John Crosland, but before we will call this witness, let me discuss with you some important procedural matters. First, the 92 ter document requested to be admitted by Prosecution motion of 12th of April, 2007, together with annex A and confidential annexes B and C, seems not to be object of any objection by the Defence. Am I right? So I see nodding, and so it is admitted. Please, Madam Registrar, would you assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As to the related documents, this is the folder from Limaj case P92 and the second folder with exhibits of non-DipTels and DipTels. We will certainly not be in a position to decide about admission, as we did not have the chance to read it. Any short comments from the Defence? Otherwise, if there would be longer comments or objections, you would be invited to do it in writing. Thank you. And the third point is the statement of 19th of April, dated the 20th of April but I suppose it's the 19th of April, which we received today. I see it not necessary to discuss it right now, as the issues contained will be elaborated in a more detailed way during the testimony, I would suppose, also in a more sourced and explained way viva voce. So I wonder if we can start with the witness. Just as a reminder, just as a reminder, Madam Registrar, as to the protective measures for the witness, Judge Orie already pointed out yesterday the measures which apply from other cases are still in place, and -- but we will start in open court, I understand. And so please, Madam Usher, would you escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Am I correct in my understanding that with regard to the protective measures that apply to Colonel Crosland that that's only face distortion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That's face distortion and that is also the date and place of his birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Am I right, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, you're completely correct. While the witness is coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I would remind the Chamber in relation to the exhibits from the Limaj case those DipTels from British government, they were all provided to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- subject to Rule 70 and were all and remain under seal in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But the contents of them would be basically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- the contents of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please, before we start, would you be so kind and take the declaration in the text -- the declaration, the text of which is presented to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. And, Mr. Re, it's your floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, retired Colonel John Crosland. Can you please give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: John Harry Crosland.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you're a retired British military officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you had some 37 years of experience in the British military. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And before we go on, I'll just inform you that the transcript of your testimony in the Limaj case is in evidence, and that contains a lot of the material which is relevant to the current case. In that, at the very beginning, there is some reference to who you are, but I'd just like you to put on the public record some details about who you are and where you came from if you could just briefly go back to when you joined the British army and just tell the Trial Chamber a very brief synopsis of your career.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I see. I was commissioned from Sandhurst in 1967 into the parachute regiment. I remained with the parachute regiment for four years before transferring into the special forces and I remained throughout with the special forces and the parachute regiment until I retired in late 2001. In 1996, I was appointed as the Defence Attache to the former Republic of Yugoslavia, where I was accredited to the Vojska Jugoslavije, the VJ, and in particular to General Perisic, who was then the Chief of the General Staff. I served in Belgrade until 1999 when NATO bombed and I then returned with the Rapid Reaction Corps as a liaison officer to General Jackson when NATO forces went back into the province of Kosovo and I remained there until about mid-June of 1999. I subsequently returned to Belgrade in 2000 to help re-set up the British embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please tell the Chamber briefly about your military action combat, tours of duty.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I have been fortunate, or otherwise, to have had a lot of combat experience, both in counter-insurgency and counter-revolutionary warfare as well as several other wars throughout the Middle East, the Balkans and elsewhere as classified areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your career in the army how many soldiers did you have under your command at various times?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I commanded at regimental level and above to brigade level which is approximately 4 to 5.000 men and the equivalent equipment as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What languages do you speak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Apart from English, I speak, Serbian, French, German, I have some Arabic and Russian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what your experience is with weaponry, the extent of your -- if you could summarise the extent of your knowledge about weaponry employed in western armies and armies in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As an infantry -- primarily infantry and special forces officer, I'm familiar with most small-arms and I've trained in the heavier arms in the machine-guns and in the rocket and rocket-propelled grenade area. I am not completely qualified to -- to give, you know, very intense evidence, because that needs a qualified armourer in our army, so I'm not an armourer. I'm a general purpose officer who's had a lot of experience within weapons systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is your experience in relation to the types of arms and weapons employed by groups opposed to armies such as the British army in things such as counter-insurgency or insurgency operations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Normally a counter-insurgency force will, in its fledgling state, attempt to, what I would use, shoot-and-scoot tactics. Very rarely will they want to take on a professional fighting force for the obvious reasons that they usually do not have the heavy weapons and the variety of weapons and the range of weapons to take on these forces. So they will use possibly sniper rifles or ordinary rifles to inflict casualties and then to fade away into the undergrowth and attack when the time is right for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm taking you to your -- the job you had in the former Yugoslavia -- sorry, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as the Defence Attache. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what -- what your duties were.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, sir, I was accredited to the Vojska Jugoslavije on behalf of our Chief of the General Staff directly to then-General Perisic and we would work through the Foreign Liaison Service, which was the official channels through which we would conduct our business, whatever that happened to be. When the situation began to develop in Kosovo, I then had several conversations with senior people, as I think you're well aware from my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What does a Defence Attache do or what did you do as a Defence Attache in Yugoslavia between 1996 and 1999? What was the job description and what did it involve is what I'm getting at?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As the Defence Attache you are accredited to the armed forces of that country, the military, and you're there to help and advise your ambassador, if the need arise, and to accompany him on various political missions if there is a military input required.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The ambassador at that time, the relevant time, Sir Brian Donnelly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and before him, Sir Ivor Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What restrictions were placed upon your movement as a UK Defence Attache in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: All attaches, as I said, went through the Foreign Liaison Service, FLS, and any journey that you required to do outside of I think it was 120 miles from Belgrade had to be rooted through the Foreign Liaison Service for permission to be granted and for your own safety to be ensured. So the Vojska Jugoslavije would know of all my trips into the province of Kosovo and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: During the period you were the Defence Attache until you left, I think it was the 23rd of March, 1999, approximately how many trips did you make to Kosovo in your capacity as the Defence Attache?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think I'm correct in saying, sir, I made about 70 to 75, of which those reports are with the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you get from Belgrade to Kosovo on those trips?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We drove, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who's "we"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I would usually go with a further colleague, sometimes the American, Canadian, Dutch, French, or German attaches or on my own with my own assistant, UK assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever have an armed escort when you went to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, sir. We travelled in civilian clothes. All we had was our "licna karta," which is the identity card. We were never armed, and we were in -- or laterally, I was in a very visible bright red armoured defender with Union Jacks on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you become aware of the existence of the KLA or the UCK, the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I carried out my first trip to Kosovo, sir, in about August 1996, and there was -- there were rumours that there was some kind of fledgling military wing from Albania. I think one would say that didn't really blossom into anything until late 1997/early 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the sources of your information about the existence of the organisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In the early days, this was based on intelligence reports that we received from our own Ministry of Defence and other allied attaches' intelligence, and also, I think, just talking in general to people down in the province of Kosovo where the Albanian problem was starting to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you also receive intelligence information, military intelligence information, from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir. When in -- particularly in early 1998, when the Vojska Jugoslavije was getting concerned over the emergence of the Kosovo Liberation Army, we were then briefed on a couple of occasions, at least, of incidents that had occurred on the -- primarily on the Albanian border, but also there were indications that there was smuggling on the Macedonian border as well. But as you're well aware, both these borders have been used for smuggling from ancient times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I didn't want to overlap, but that would be interesting what do you mean by "the Albanian problem" that was starting to appear, you said. Was it what you then described? Or is it to complicate it to answer with one sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The notion is a little bit foggy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. By "the Albanian problem," I suppose we mean the emergence of a very young, fledgling Kosovo Liberation Army. It wasn't actually -- I didn't think it was called that at the time, but there were indications through intelligence sources that people were -- were coming together to put the basis for this organisation together, sir, if that helps. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to understand you better. Please, Mr. Re, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A few moments ago you said that you were aware of the existence -- or you had heard rumours of the existence of the organisation but it didn't blossom -- really blossom into anything until 1997/1998. What was this blossoming-into process? What were you aware of by the end of 1997/1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, as I mentioned in my report, sir, that we had meetings with Colonel-General Dimitrijevic, who was head of counter-intelligence, in late 1997, and General Perisic, who were disturbed by reports coming from both the Albanian and the Macedonian border that men and materiels were being moved. And then in early 1998, the first attacks took place against the MUP stations in Kosovo itself, and if I remember correctly, they were based -- they were against the MUP station at Rudnik and Likosane. And that's when the first -- as far as I'm aware, the first Serbian security force casualties were taken. I may be wrong on that, but I think that is the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How does that accord with what you described earlier as I think shoot-and-scoot-type activities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, the first -- following on from the attacks on the MUP station at Rudnik where I think three policemen were killed, the Serbian authorities decided to take action at Donji Prekaz and carried out a very blunt and aggressive attack against the Jashari family in March 1998. And this was the start of -- I would say this was the start of the contest-proper between the Kosovo Liberation Army and the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what the reason for the attack on the MUP station was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think the KLA then, as I said, was a very young organisation and saw, as in many countries in the world, the police stations are in the middle of towns or villages and are, therefore, very -- potentially very soft targets. The policemen are just doing their job in maintaining law and order, and the one at -- the police station particularly at Rudnik is in a valley and is overlooked all the way around and therefore a very easy target to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to elaborate a bit more on what you described a moment ago as "the start of the contest-proper between the Kosovo Liberation Army and the Serbian security forces." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, I think the attack on the Jashari compound at Donji Prekaz, which I then took a whole crowd of ambassadors and other people to look at the damage done, and the compound was virtually razed to the ground. Very heavy fighting had taken place. Very heavy use of force had taken place against the Jashari family, which, as I understand it, it was adjudged by the Serbian authorities to be a family that was heavily engaged in various nefarious activities or business activities, shall we put it like that, including armed aggression. I think this was to attempt to teach the Kosovo Liberation Army a lesson.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to focus a little bit on "contest-proper", and if you could just elaborate on what you mean by "contest-proper." "Contest" has a connotation of there being sides to some sort of altercation. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs turned up for this particular match with very extremely heavy use of force and numbers of men. The Jashari family decided to stand and fight and suffered very heavily, and I think the KLA learnt their lesson that -- in particularly in the countryside in the Drenica, where this event took place, was not the area to take the Serbian security forces on because it's very open and favours the side that has the heavier and out-ranging fire-power that the Serbs had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the relative strengths on both sides in this particular contest, that's at the Jashari family compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think in my report we saw 55 -- or 54 bodies were returned to the Donji Prekaz area, Kosovo Albanian bodies. The exact strength I don't know of the rest of the Kosovo connection. The Serbian security forces were probably numbering in the hundreds, probably 1500 to 2.000 men, and armoured vehicles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of -- what sort of resistance did the -- did those on the otherwise put up to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: From what I understand, sir, they fought where they were, and then attempted to escape and were shot. The details I can't give you because, obviously, no one was there when this particular happened. We came in a couple of days after -- after this particular incident had taken place and when the bodies were returned from Pristina morgue, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information at that time about the number of Serb military personnel in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The Vojska Jugoslavije order of battle, as we call it, for province of Kosovo was under 52 corps, based in Pristina, which had approximately between 10 and 15.000 men stationed in the province of Kosovo itself. This was obviously supplemented by the Ministry of the Interior Police, the MUP, and that rose up and down depending on the situation but probably got as high, again, to 10 to 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What weaponry did the VJ have at its disposal in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The Vojska Jugoslavije had the full range from main battle tank down to armoured personnel carrier, down to triple anti-aircraft weapons that could be used in the ground role and all the normal infantry and heavy -- both light and heavy weapons. So they had the full spectrum of weapons systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just as a matter of clarification, the question asks: "What weaponry did the VJ have at its disposal in that area?" Which might be understood to mean in the Drenica area where the attack on the Jashari compound occurred or in the province of Kosovo as a whole. Now, it might be helpful just to have matters like that clarified as the questions are asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Crosland --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While we're on the same subject matter I understand that some 54 bodies were recovered. It might be of some assistance to determine how many of those bodies were able-bodied fighting men as opposed to women or children or older or younger people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That is an additional question, but just to make clear what you mean by the area. You first were speaking of the province of Kosovo. Mr. Crosland, was that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The army unit, the Vojska Jugoslavije unit, within Kosovo was 52 corps, which had the whole spectrum of weaponry. In the Drenica region itself, as I recall and like is in my report, sir, this is primarily a MUP operation, initially. Now, as I say, I was not there for the operation, so I cannot say whether the Vojska Jugoslavije was involved in this or not, but within this operation the police had armoured personnel carriers and the air defence weapons systems that are extremely useful for house fight -- house fighting and so on in a very heavy manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Re, do you want to elaborate on what Mr. Guy-Smith was asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will clarify Mr. Guy-Smith's query.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something in relation to that last answer before I get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And, Colonel Crosland, did the VJ have a similar capacity, capacity, in the Drenica area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: At that time, if my memory serves me right, I think the primacy was still with the MUP and therefore the VJ was on the outside. And as far as I recall and remember, they were not engaged in this particular operation, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In relation to the 54 bodies and the clarification sought there, did you see the bodies yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: If I remember rightly - and again, I think it's in one of my reports - most of these bodies had been shot at close range, which could indicate they were -- had been murdered because it's unusual for everyone to be -- have a head shot or a face shot. There was a range of - and this again is purely from memory, Your Honour - there was a range of personnel from fairly elderly people down to and including, if I remember correctly, young children. But there was certainly people of fighting age within this group of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long after their deaths did you see them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, sir, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Please, Mr. Re, we have all to slow down a little bit not to make the work of the translators too difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the question now, to be honest. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long after the deaths did you see the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, sir, the bodies were returned, as we were told, from Pristina morgue and dumped on the outskirts of Srbica, if I remember rightly, and I think that was maybe a couple or three days after the incident had taken place. We came -- I came down with the United States Defence Attache and we were the only two people who were allowed into the operational area to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were any -- or do you remember whether any of the bodies were dressed in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not as far as I can recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you first become aware that the KLA had a fighting capacity?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Again, recalling from my report, sir, I think in the early part of 1998 after the Jashari incident in the Drenica valley activities took a bit of a dip, and then the KLA started to become more prominent towards the end of March, into May -- April and May. And by about -- I think I'm right in recalling by the middle of May they were, as I've said in the report, technically controlling about 50, 60 per cent of Kosovo in the way that they -- they blocked three of the four main routes across Kosovo with fairly limited forces, but it showed that they did have the ability to deploy various groups into strategic areas to impinge on Serbian security forces actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to elaborate a bit more on what you mean by technically controlling. And I assume you're talking in a military sense here. If you're not, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, you're right, sir. As I said, there are four major routes across the province of Kosovo from Pristina in the east and Mitrovica and Urosevac to the key areas which are in the west from Prizren, Djakovica, and up towards Pec. And three of these routes were blocked, the most northern route at Rakos just west of Rudnik, the central main route from Pristina in the area of Likosane going towards Pec. The southern -- one of the southern routes was blocked just beyond Stimlje towards Crnoljevo leaving the Urosevac -- or what I would call the mountain route into Prizren as the only route through which the Serbs could carry out a resupply. The routes were blocked by fairly -- sorry. The routes were blocked by lightly armed forces who'd -- would ambush the roads, pull a vehicle across the road, and dig fairly shallow trenches as a token defensive position around the area. So it was a control tactic, in effect, that was a rebuff, really, to the far superior Serbian potential fire-power and formations that they had available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did they manage to achieve the 50 to 60 per cent control -- or technical control of Kosovo in this way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think because it took the Serbian security forces that length of time to adjust to the fact that there was a fledgling organisation that was creating problems in the province of Kosovo. I think they were primarily concentrating their initial energies on the Albanian -- on the western border with Albania and also looking after the Macedonian border which, as I've said before, were the two major routes through which men and materiels were passed to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you experience or encounter these KLA blocks resulting in the technical control of 50 to 60 per cent of Kosovo in your own trips to Kosovo during that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. We travelled throughout the area despite the attempted blockage by the KLA, who at certain stages would not recognise our "licna karta," and usually after some negotiation, possibly over a glass of whisky, we would get where we wanted to get to and they would remain where they wanted to remain. So it was a fairly fluid, in both terms, situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just clarify what a licna karta is for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. "Licna karta" is the Serbian for identity card, which is the identity card we were issued with by the Foreign Liaison Service to identify us as personnel who had the right to travel throughout the -- Yugoslavia, and therefore could -- should not be stopped by anyone unless it was a Vojska Jugoslavije or MUP for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, I hope this isn't an unhelpful interjection. A few questions ago Mr. Re asked what the witness meant by the word "technically" in the phrase "technically in control." And I wonder whether that question might be pursued so that we will understand what "technically" means in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it's of assistance to the Trial Chamber, I can pursue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, can you elaborate on what you mean by "technical control."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: When -- yes, Your Honour, gentlemen. When you have a road blocked by 20 or 30 fighters with pretty light weapons and ammunition and very little with which to defend themselves, I would suggest that if they were approached by a column of tanks or armoured vehicles, the most sensible thing would be to disappear. What for some reason I can't answer that - the only people who can answer the question is the Vojska Jugoslavije - is why they allowed relatively light forces - and therefore I use the word "technically" - to close a road, which the Serbian security forces had massive power with which to open these roads as soon as they were "technically" closed. So what you have is a very light force blocking the road, causing a problem which really shouldn't be a problem. I hope that clarifies that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: If you're satisfied, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the situation on the road between Pec and Djakovica March, April, May, June, July 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In the western area, so the international boundary, as everybody's perfectly aware, is in the mountains between Albania and Serbia, then Kosovo, the province of Kosovo. It's an extremely difficult, not to say, demanding area. It goes up several -- I think 3.000 metres, 9, 10.000 in feet. It's extremely cold in winter, minus 20, minus 30, and it's plus 30 in the summer. So it's a testing geographical boundary to try and guard and prevent men and materiels being pushed through on routes that were known about for ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Crosland, could you focus on the situation between March and July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And on the Pec to Djakovica road.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. With great respect, I think it is relevant because the Serbs were unable to hold the mountain, and therefore moved a second boundary back along to the road between Prizren-Djakovica-Decani, and this became what I would call -- refer to the front line or the thin red line where the Serbs attempted to prevent the ever-growing flow of men and materiels in late 1998 through this area. And so this road became an important road, along which there were many battles fought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Once more, please, you were not talking of late 1998 and can you describe that or refer to March, April, May, June, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the Vojska Jugoslavije and the MUP realised the importance of this area and the -- the Pec-Decani-Djakovica-Prizren road as a corridor which they had to attempt to hold, and that was pertinent in early 1998 and throughout 1998 into 1999. It therefore, as I say, became a second frontier, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you yourself travel on that road in the period March to July 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Most of the time, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you encounter KLA presence in your travels along that road?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Approximately how many times do you think you travelled along that road in either direction in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly, sir, but my reports would indicate the route, as we always state in the report. We would stay in either Pec, Djakovica, or in Prizren overnight in order to be able to travel throughout the area of Kosovo as and when trouble flared up. So we were there -- or I was there, rather, for the majority of the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In terms of numbers, are we talking 10, 20, 30, 40, 100, 5, what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Are you referring to the strength of the KLA, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. The times you went backwards and forwards on that road. I appreciate it's been a long time but approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I would say it's well over a hundred times, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We had the number of 70 to 75 trips from Belgrade to the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In the overall period, and so maybe -- to what period are you now referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: March to July 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: These four or five months, would that be then -- the relevant portion of that 70 trips?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As in also, if I may explain it, into other areas. So part of the process to get to know the situation on the ground, we travelled around and around and around areas all day long from first light until last night and even after at times. So in some days we may go up and down that road three or four times. So it was an extensive use. The reason for that, sir, was to attempt to monitor the situation and report it as fairly as possible on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Describe the KLA presence you encountered on that road between March and July 1998.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The major areas on that road were in the area of Prilep and Rznic, which is right in the middle, and that was a very disputed area ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, that was a very disputed area, so that was the major area where we would see KLA activity. There was also some activity just south of the major town in the north, Pec, and along the disputed villages in Decani, Gornji Streoc, and also on the outskirts of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the KLA activity you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In the early part of 1998, it was mainly restricted to shoot-and-scoot-type tactics, sniper attacks on this road, because that was the main supply route for the Serbian security forces, and therefore with the vehicle check-points, security points, that is, the Serbian security forces put in, these would offer static targets against which the KLA could plan, as I say, sniper attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to have a map, a sort of new map on e-court so that we -- because there are quite a lot of names mentioned. It might be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Yeah, we can use the hard ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That's fine. And I take it, sir, you have a map in front of yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: For reconstruction of your memory. And is this, may I ask, Mr. Re, a document of the Prosecution or is it a private map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I was simply going to say it might be helpful if we were all following the evidence on the same map. I see Colonel Crosland has his own map and some have maps in hard copy. I believe unless I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- mistaken, that the larger map we have been focusing on is in the e-court system and can be brought up on the screen and that way indeed, if necessary, Colonel Crosland can mark it on the screen for us if he wants to point a particular place out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree. Would that be a way, Mr. Re? Could we load it up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: P10 is the map of immediate importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So that the witness can sign it and mark it. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, if you could have a look at the map which will come up on the screen in a moment and I will ask you to mark on - it may seem fairly obvious - the road between Pec and Djakovica, which is of main concern to me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the extract of it. The one I want is this one without the red circles on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I've certainly no objection to the circled map being used, if that would assist. It's obviously not necessarily the same places that Colonel Crosland would be referring to; and if all else fails, we could take a hard copy and put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. That would certainly be useful, but it's up to you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just can't recall the number of the map. I think it's coming. 1006.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could it be that it is Exhibit P32?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's a map in front of you; it has circles on it. It's --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you assist me with the exhibit number for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit Number D32.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the court officer, Colonel, could you just mark with the -- on the -- with the magic pen the road.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The road we are -- Your Honour, what we're talking about is from Pec up here, all the way down to Decani. And there were various villages around Decani, Gornji Streoc and places that were fought over throughout March -- May 1998. Then come on down below Decani to the area of Prilep and Rznic, which are just in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you. And then on down to the west you've got the town of Junik which saw a lot of action in 1998 throughout, which is just here close to the border. The road goes on then down very straight on down towards Djakovica, which is off the map as it stands at the moment. So that is the road, Your Honour, that I was talking about as the sort of secondary boundary and resupply route that was being used by the Serbian security forces and which was fought over by both sides throughout 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: While the map's still there, I want you to describe to the Court what the KLA presence was, I mean, in terms of numbers of soldiers or civilians or whatever you saw and where you saw them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In the -- the early stages of 1998, I think there were several groupings of KLA throughout the area of Kosovo, in particular in this area, in the Dukadjin area, as I understand it or understood it, when we got further intelligence from various outside agencies, we started to put together areas of operational responsibility, as the military call it. We try and group things or people into areas and make people or -- or people then become or appear to become responsible for those particular areas. And this was the Dukadjin area which stretched from -- in the north Pec, in the north, through Decani down to Djakovica, and then around in a big loop. I can put it on the map if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You could. Do you have -- is there another coloured pen you could use for that. Maybe you could use a --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What choices do we have? Blue? Right. Let's use black.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. We're coming from Djakovica, which is down here, then we go up through an area called Rakovina, and on up to main junction of the road where Klina is, and this is of the road to Pristina. And then it goes westwards into Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if I might, just again, clarity on these matters is extremely important. The answer at page 25, line 8, begins by referring to the early stages of 1998, and then moves on to a point which further intelligence was obtained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that being the point at which an attempt was made to reconstruct areas of operational responsibility. It may be important to know when it was that that further intelligence was obtained, giving rise to that understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Please, could you ask in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you clarify the question Mr. Emmerson has just put to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, gentlemen, as far as I can recall, I think there was a -- a UK assessment of the potential KLA threat, I think - and I'm trying to recall now from nearly whatever it is 12 years ago. I think it was in April or even May of 1998. It may be referred to in my previous documents but I'm not quite certain, but I think that was about roughly when we tried to put some kind of organisation of battle on to a -- what was then a fledgling organisation, the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were drawing a black territorial line around what you said was the Dukadjin area. Have you finished drawing it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, I haven't, because it came -- excuse me. It came back down the Pec line, down to Djakovica --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the moment you're drawing the black over the blue, you're using the same axis, that is the road from Pec to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, with respect, it's not as tidy as that because the area of operations, obviously, included the western border in the mountains to Albania, and that was, in itself, part of the Dukadjin -- what came to be called the Dukadjin area. So it would come down -- there is a big pass, the Rugova pass up here which goes up into Montenegro and to Crna Gora which again had an influence in this area. This mountainous area, here, was also involved in activities and also likewise in this area here, again, along the Albanian-Kosovo border. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So may we -- maybe we should note that the witness marked first in the left upper corner with an R, the Rugova pass, then went down and entered this arrow at the side and then at the left-down corner, all with black pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this would have -- this -- this, with respect, Your Honour, this area of operations would go on down south from Djakovica all the way down to Prizren, which had the exit down towards Kukes in Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it -- it is a large area which I've attempted to define, but it -- with respect to the Court, it's not like a backyard in America, it's not fenced-in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just going back to what I was asking you a little while ago, and that is what you saw, I want you to tell the Court what you saw between March and July 1998 in terms of KLA presence along that particular road. What were your own observations with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We -- if I think -- if my memory is correct, we had a meeting with a gentleman called Ramush Haradinaj, at his headquarters in Glodjane area near Rznic. We would see evidence of KLA fighting, particularly in the Rznic-Prilep area, as I've indicated before, and then sporadic fighting all the way down that road from south of Pec, around Decani, Rznic-Prilep-Junik, down. Further down from Junik, there is a place called Ponosevac here, which was a Vojska Jugoslavije-MUP position, and again there would be indications of both KLA activity and MUP activity in this area. Because of the sensitivity of the border area through which men and materiels were being -- were starting to be moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've marked something on the map. Can you please put a P next to the crescent that you've drawn so we know it's Ponosevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I was just asking -- about to ask you, Mr. Re, if we then should save this marked map in this way or if you would like to continue with markings. But we should not take it off the screen before saving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I might ask the witness to mark something on the road line which he's just referred to in his evidence, so I'd like to keep it up at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, if you just draw a P next to that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This map is a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I know it's not easy.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: -- unclear from where I'm seeing it but I think that's the area of Ponosevac there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You described having to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure and it is difficult to see the map in this particular magnification, but I think I'm right in saying that Ponosevac is further south than that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- And it may be if the witness is focusing in on Ponosevac we would need to save this and then -- because we have to save it before magnifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and then allow him to magnify it to clarify his evidence, because I think he-- I may be wrong, but I think it he may have put the P some considerable distance further north than Ponosevac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you are correct, Mr. Emmerson. Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please, Madam Registrar, can we mark that -- can we save that and keep it. That would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P70, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then next step would be to move and enlarge the map to what we are addressing now. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It might be easier to give the witness a hard copy of the map; we've certainly got a few in court. I can provide him with my -- I've got a copy of the court copy here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's just much easier to read on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That means we finished now with the marking exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, you are definitely free to open another map then later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, did you encounter in your trips along that road in that period, March to July 1998, KLA presence on the road? If so, I want you to describe to the Trial Chamber what you saw -- soldiers, civilians, or whatever -- roadblocks, whatever you saw.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We would see fairly small groups of KLA in the area of Rznic Prilep and also on the outskirts of Djakovica that would occasionally try and prevent our access into the areas. But usually they were there. They were not -- obviously they were very lightly armed and they knew they were in the presence of superior Serb security forces, which were being held quite local -- or locally, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you know that they were KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Because the majority of them would be wearing uniform with KLA badges.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the size of these small groups?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I would say initially maybe 10 to 15 men, sometimes a bit bigger if we went off down towards Glodjane where there was -- appeared to be some kind of headquarters. There may be 30 men there. I visited other KLA headquarters in the Drenica and further east, and again there were the similar types of people, quantities of people, apart from Malisevo, where there was about 100 -- 100, 150 personnel, which I think is reported in one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they lightly armed with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: At this -- in the -- in early 1998 we saw mainly light infantry weapons, rifles, revolvers, some light machine-guns. So they were very lightly armed. The odd rocket grenade, propelled grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about where they were obtaining their weapons from and how they were getting these weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think the general feeling was that when Albania had imploded in 1997, that the majority of weaponry had come from Albanian sources and as, I'm sure, you're aware, the Balkans is awash with weapons from many, many countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You used the word "feeling." What was your information or the source of information about where the weapons were coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, if I remember correctly, that was from Ministry of Defence intelligence assessments and from the -- also from the Vojska Jugoslavije, who, as I said, did brief us on at least two occasions as to the growing severity of KLA incursions into then what was sovereign Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about how the weapons were getting into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Again, the -- there were -- there were well-known routes across the Albanian-Kosovo border that had been used since the silk trade, so these were the obvious routes through which arms, men and materiel, would come. Some of these routes were blocked by both Vojska Jugoslavije on the frontier, on the border itself; by outposts. But unless you patrol in a fairly aggressive manner, then you can sit in a static position and all you see is what you can see. And when it gets dark, you don't see a great deal. So a lot of stuff can get by with a bit of ingenuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did any of these routes cross through the Dukadjin area, which you have drawn on the exhibit a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. As I was saying, these are the historic smuggling routes, and a lot of them went through the Dukadjin route in order to resupply the Drenica area of operations just to the west of Pristina, and also going further up to -- to the east of Kosovo, Mitrovica, to the KLA based up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the significance of the Dukadjin area in terms of the smuggling of weapons from Albania?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Over the Albanian border in areas of Kukes and Crmljane it was well-known that there were training camps, and I think even the -- if I remember rightly, the Vojska Jugoslavije informed me that they had information of these major training centres in Albania which were feeding and supplying the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But what was the significance of the Dukadjin area, if it -- indeed it had any?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As, I think, again I have indicated in my reports, that it became the prime area because it was the main resupply route from Kosovo through -- sorry, from Albania through to Kosovo, and the control of that route with the major cities of Pec, Decani, and Djakovica, and Prizren were the four major towns in that area. And therefore, if the KLA wished to influence the area in the future, then they needed to have some kind of control in the area. I think what you must understand is that in all these towns there was a very, very heavy Serbian military presence. So saying that the KLA had control has got to be tempered with the fact that they were initially probably the goldfish in the bowl, but very rapidly the Serbs became the goldfish in the bowl with a local population, not necessarily backing the KLA, but because the population -- majority of the population is Albanian, then they had more influence in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I'm not that familiar with the colloquialism of a goldfish in a bowl. Could you clarify that a little.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The point I'm trying to make is that the majority of the population within Kosovo, as a whole, was probably approaching a million or a million and a half Albanian or Kosovo Albanian, to probably only about -- probably 250 to 450.000 Serbs. So while the Serbs maintained - again, I use the word technical control - the majority of the people in the area were actually Albanian, and therefore could support the Kosovo Liberation Army if they so wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you mean by the KLA were initially the goldfish in the bowl? Can you just elaborate briefly on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, as I stated quite a few times in my reports, that a lot of the Albanians, whether Kosovo or just ordinary Albanians within Kosovo, really did not want either interference from the Serbian security forces or from 1998 onwards, the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You described smuggling routes. What do you mean by "routes"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, these are trails through the mountains that are being used to carry cigarettes, contraband of all sorts, and then from the two major bases of Bajram Curri and Kukes they would set off with -- as 1998 rolled on, both men and materiels would be -- would be sent across the mountains either on pack-horses or donkeys as a way of getting supplies into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able on either -- to draw either on the map which was on the screen a moment ago, or on any of the maps which are in that binder to your right, where the smuggling routes were and how they went into the Dukadjin area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I can't draw precisely, no. I mean, these were routes that -- I mean, for instance, in the area of -- if we go to Junik -- which map are we on now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's a map to your right which is the same map, it's on the ELMO, and it's a paper copy.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: If you go into the town -- into the area of Junik, you will see some very light black hachuring that goes down into Junik, both north and south. These were two mountain trails that led out of Junik across the border into Kosovo. There were many other trails. If you go down towards Ponosevac, and then -- this map doesn't go quite far enough because the border is not shown. Again there are trails that come across. So these are the types of trails that the KLA used, obviously, to try and avoid the known Vojska Jugoslavije and Serb positions on the border. Further down by Djakovica and on down towards Mount Pastrik, that mountain was crisscrossed with trails that were used to infiltrate men and materiels with. So they used whatever trail was available and which they did not think would be observed by the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to your right, on the ELMO, there is a binder of maps, of various maps of Kosovo, which cross the Albanian border. If you could just perhaps flick through those and if you can find one which you could indicate -- give a better indication where these routes are.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: So the best map is -- which doesn't actually show the Albanian side but goes to the border is west Kosovo -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We might -- we should find a way to make a break like quarter to 4.00. Would you then tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you just -- what's the number on the map -- on the bottom of that map, the green one? It should say court map --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Map 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. You're looking at court map 4. Are you able to draw roughly, with a marker, where these routes were, just with arrows? It doesn't need to be precisely --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, with respect, what one has got to understand is that these routes are not like the auto route to Schiphol Airport. These are just trails that some are very old. Others are just footpaths as well. So it's -- what I can indicate to you is that if you come up towards Pec and follow the road -- the track up into the mountains into the pass west of Pec, you'll get over into Montenegro. That is quite a major dirt road. Alongside it there are many trails which refugees have used and which were used as well for passage both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, what I'd like you to do is to actually draw with a black pen what you've just marked so we have a clear record of what you're referring to. Blue is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Do you mean the witness should mark it in the map book in this map number 4, which is not -- which is not to scale, which is a problematic map, actually, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's not to scale but it is an approximation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It would be quite sufficient I think to have it in a verbal description, but on the other hand, Mr. Crosland, maybe you can give us an idea of where your knowledge from these historic routes comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the route I've just indicated to Your Honour from Pec across through the Rugova pass is a route which the -- in fact, the Serbian army withdrew over in the first world war. So it is a major route, but alongside this major route there would be several footpaths in the hills which were known to both sides of locals which they would use to pass backwards and forwards between in this case Montenegro and Serbia. If we move down towards the small town of Morina here which was a post, a Vojska Jugoslavije border post, the town of Batusa and Kosare, you will see Junik up here. As I've indicated there are trails out of Junik. There are trails going west out of Kosare, and also there is a trail that goes across the Morina pass, which was a Vojska Jugoslavije position. If I remember when I was up there, either side of this position at Morina, we saw other trails that were -- have obviously been frequently used by people and animals carrying men and materiels backwards and forwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you go on down to Djakovica, again there was a major crossing point, if I remember correctly, I think in this area below Zulfaj, which again has a Vojska Jugoslavije position on it. Again, either side of that there were trails that indicated movement. And then down towards Prizren on the mount on Pastrik mountain, which is in this area here, a large mountain, there were several trails across the border itself. So I hope that gives you some idea of the complex nature of trying to prevent infiltration both ways in this area, this frontier area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Should we keep this in a form as a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I want to keep it as a form. I just want the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, you just marked -- you put sort of a line between the arrow and Pastrik. Can you just make that larger, like put an arrow on it, so that it's quite clear when you've gone? Zulfaj was the name of the town you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This is Zulfaj is up here. We then go further --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah. All I want you to do is so that we can see when you've gone --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- where you've actually marked if you could go back to Zulfaj and put the arrow over the border as well if that's in fact --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: So this -- these arrows should all go both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. Just noting that these were approximate smuggling areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Absolutely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Might that be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So would that be an appropriate moment? So can we first give a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this will be Exhibit Number P71, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I indicate that I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: There's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There isn't an objection as such at all. It's simply that at some point, either when Mr. Re resumes if he thinks it right, or at some later stage it would be appropriate, we would submit, for Colonel Crosland to be invited to indicate smuggling routes in other areas of Kosovo, for example, across the Macedonian border and in from the north in Montenegro to get a sense of -- I think Mr. Re's point that he's seeking to elicit from this is relative importance. And so I don't know whether that is the map that's appropriate. With an electronic map, once saved, it cannot be retrieved, whereas with that map, of course, or other maps it can be marked subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, the Bench agrees. Can you think about that in a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll certainly think about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So court adjourns until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I was thinking we should talk about time. Are you aware of a limited time budget you will have to finish with your examination-in-chief, at least today if not before the end of the third session. That will depend on your intention to introduce certain documents you will consider essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, if I could perhaps be given an indication of how long I've taken. Can the registry give me that indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: To my estimate it will be 1 hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Until so far you had 80 minutes. What is your intention?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, if I could put it this way, the -- I have, I think, maybe 70 documents or so, in addition to those in Limaj, which were read on -- but basically the main parts were read on to the transcript in Limaj. There's about another 70 documents that I wish to introduce or have the witness comment on in some form. Now, the math with that are if I show them to the witness even in the hard copy, it takes him three minutes per document, it will take many hours more to do it. Now, clearly within the time budgeted or allowed, I can't do it in that form. So my proposal was to take him to the parts of the evidence I have to lead orally in relation to the Lake Radonjic canal visit and so on, and to have him look at his exhibits and to comment selectively on some of them and to get as many in as I possibly can that way. That just means I can't get him to illuminate or put into perspective a lot of the DipTels and yes, I -- of course to do it I'd need more than the three hours allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. So you get started maybe again and go as far to the point as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, the next thing -- if we could just return briefly to what we were -- what you were giving your testimony about before, and that was the road between Pec and Djakovica. You referred to some roadblocks on that road. Now, in the time you travelled on it in March to July 1998, did you ever encounter KLA roadblocks on that particular road?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The reason I'm not answering directly is that I don't think they were ever an official roadblock. There might be some KLA stood by the side of the road or at a turning that would stop the traffic, but it would be literally men, a few men, carrying out an impromptu vehicle check, as it were, and then they would disappear again. Because as I've indicated to the Court, that up and down this road there were very considerable Serbian security forces deployed all the way along it. So it was a question of the KLA choosing a random point to make an impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about control of the road in that period? Are you able to say whether one side or the other controlled the road?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think probably the basis of control, for want of a better word, would be -- would rest with the Serb forces. In very localised situations around Rznic and Prilep in particular then the KLA might have slightly more control for limited periods in this early sage of March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about after March 1998, as in April, May, and June 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, again, as I said, the situation was very fluid throughout the whole of 1998 until the later stages when we saw considerable more KLA activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what you mean by "fluid."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, one of the -- in my humble opinion, one of the major problems that the Serbian security forces fell into was that they would rush about and take some ground of tactical importance, take that particular piece of ground, and then decided they would withdraw back to a more secure area. Most of the time when that happened, the KLA would then, as I call it, back-fill back into their original positions. So you would have this very fluid situation where the front line, per se, would go backwards and forwards depending on who wanted to put more effort into it on that particular day and for whatever particular reason they wanted to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your knowledge or the information you had about the state of KLA organisation in that Dukadjin area in March, April, May 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, sir, as I indicated earlier that we had an initial assessment from the UK intelligence services that was trying to place throughout Kosovo the order of battle or the numbers of men and equipments or weaponry that they had to try and put some indication of the size of the KLA force that was deployed throughout Kosovo, not just in the Dukadjin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you could be a little bit more precise there. What was your information, just in that period, March, April, May 1998, of the state of organisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think I have said, sir, in reports that I looked on it as a fledgling organisation, a young organisation, with some groups more prominent than others. I would suggest that the Dukadjin group was quite -- was an important area because of what I've previously said about the men and materiel. The Drenica and then west -- sorry, east of Kosovo, Mitrovica, you have the KLA up in Bajgora. I visited throughout my time there a number of KLA headquarter elements, both in the Drenica, a place called Lausa, which is to the west of Srbica, a place called Vocnjak, the area around Klina, Lapusnik, Crni Ljug, Kraljevo, Malisevo, Bajgora to the east of Kosovska Mitrovica, and also the area of Rznic-Glodjane in the Dukadjin, and those are some of the areas I visited during my tours in the area of Kosovo and from where I made my guesstimation of the likely strengths of the KLA and at that time, as I have said on many occasions, I believed it to be approximately between 4 and 500 hard-core fighters. That -- the ranks obviously swelled during the latter part of 1998, and I think I'm correct in saying that there is a commemorative stone in Pristina to the 660 fighters that were killed, but bearing in mind I left in March 1998 when a lot of heavy fighting went on after the NATO bombing. .

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said "1998," do you mean 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, 1999, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you visit KLA headquarters in Rznic-Glodjane in the Dukadjin area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think the initial time -- first time I visited there was initiated by a political request which came from sources in Pristina, and we went across to visit KLA personnel in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I would have to refer to a document. I'm sorry, sir. I think it's in one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you remember about your visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We went down off the main road at -- in the area of Prilep-Rznic and around into the area of Glodjane, I think, and into a very typical Albanian house which had high walls and was very nicely laid out. And it was just one house within a village which, as I say, was very typical of the architecture throughout Kosovo, the province of Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, there were, sir. There were about, I think, between 15 and 20 people in uniform, but as I am trying to advise the Court that not necessarily everyone in uniform is a fighter or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I believe it was Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That was the gentleman's name that we were given to go and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you describe your meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The meeting was very cordial, very friendly. We sat around and had some chai and we discussed various topics. As I stated, this was mainly a visit engineered by political contacts, and I was there just to provide some military back-up and to take people into the visit itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very anxious not to take up any of Mr. Re's time. And the witness just gave an answer where he said not necessarily everyone in uniform is a fighter or a soldier, and I wondered if that might be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was quite clear that, as I said, there were, based on my experience of having to train and to fight, having fought against counter-revolutionary forces, many people wish to be a part of an insurgency movement, but when the time gets tough and rough a lot of people realise that they are being asked to actually lay down their lives for their particular project. And therefore, as I say, I think, as we all put on a good show, a lot of people always turn out perhaps for a wedding may not necessarily be friends of the family. So it's more in that connotation I would put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether the soldiers you saw at Ramush Haradinaj's headquarters fell into that category or were genuine soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think the majority I saw there, from memory, were well-disciplined, reasonably well-dressed, and I suspect the majority of them were probably quite serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons when you went to Haradinaj's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: If I remember rightly, we saw, as I said before, the light Kalashnikov rifles, machine-guns. There may have been the odd anti-tank propelled grenade, RPG.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you get into his area or to his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We were given the area of where it was, and we just drove in. And I think we may have even been guided in. I cannot remember. I knew the area; I didn't know exactly that particular spot as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there any Serb military or MUP presence in the area when you first went and saw Ramush Haradinaj at his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not, as far as I'm aware, no. I mean, they were on the road, as I said, but that particular day they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could we maybe retrieve the document the witness mentioned which contains the date of this visit. But while you are thinking about that, I have a little question. You were talking about high walls of this house, you mean walls around the whole property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a normal Kosovo Albanian project to have a high wall to safe-guard their families, and this was generally a building concept throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And still it was no problem to enter the property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There is a normal gate, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's like a fortified villa, as it were, which is I think throughout the Mediterranean countries is a normal practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm rising to my feet because I think Mr. Re's search on the other side of the room may be a search in vain, because I certainly know that on our side, we've searched through all of Colonel Crosland's documentation, such as it's been made available to us and we've never been able to retrieve a document dealing with the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Of course, this was no intention of mine to send Mr. Re on a search in vain. But, thank you for that remark. And, please, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That does accord with our understanding, too. We don't think we can locate such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
