utterances.text: How many times did you meet Mr. Haradinaj in the period --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, sir, I think three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Over what period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Over the period from early 1998, throughout 1998, and I think we may have met once again in Prizren when the Rapid Reaction Corps was in -- KFOR were in there dealing with the withdrawal of the Vojska Jugoslavije Brigade there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that later, when you met him in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. That was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember meeting someone called Jakup Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think that was when I met people at the headquarters in Crnoljevo or it may have been at Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Daut Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The brother -- I believe we did meet. As I say, it's -- there's an awful lot of water gone under the bridge since then, so I would not be able to recognise Daut if he was in the court or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your understanding about the extent of Haradinaj's control or command when you met him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think I'm right in saying he indicated that he controlled what was called the Dukadjin area, which is the area I'd explained and the importance of that area. And this was, I think, alluded to or confirmed, whichever word you want to, in the assessment that had been made by outside intelligence agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you give an approximation of when it was that you met him and understood that -- or he told you he controlled this area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, I think, as I said, this was March/April 1998, the initial contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, please, could you wait a few seconds after the question, as you speak the same language, it would otherwise cause a problem for the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the Lake Radonjic canal area and your visit to that area in September 1998. And I want you to tell the Trial Chamber how you came to visit the Lake Radonjic canal area.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: So we had been, as I've indicated before to the Court, staying in Djakovica at the Pastrik Hotel. And I think we were called, if I recall -- remember rightly by KDOM, Kosovo Verification Mission, and the MUP and asked to go with them to witness a massacre site, in their terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just stop you there. Who is "we"? Who were you with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: With the American Defence Attache.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that Bill Fisher?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That was Bill Fisher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I recall, we drove there in convoy with the MUP, a lieutenant-colonel from Djakovica, and they headed the convoy and we turned in with them at Prilep. And from Prilep in towards Rznic, there was an intense operation still ongoing with elements of both the MUP; their special -- their special police, the PJP; and also elements of the Vojska Jugoslavije, with tanks and armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by a special operation -- I'm sorry, an intense operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot of military or security force activity from the junction of the main road turning in towards Prilep and beyond to Rznic. Both villages had been severely damaged, intensively damaged, and was still being looted as we drove past. Animal fodder was being burnt and many animals household animals -- farm animals had also been slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see any KLA presence on the road from Djakovica to Rznic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not as far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing any KLA presence in the area in which there had been the intense operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not at that specific time. This is about 4.00 in the afternoon, if I recall, and the operation, as I put in my report, to me was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was what you saw consistent with there having been a battle between different sides or with something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. There seemed to be a major -- what we'd call it, in military terms, a clearance operation along this particular axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which axis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The -- from the main road to Prilep and Rznic and then on --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, and then on to the area of the canal bank, which is into the area behind Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "military clearance operation"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, there were -- there was, as I indicated, there were heavy military forces and MUP forces literally physically moving from house to house clearing this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about who controlled that area before the MUP and the VJ moved in literally, physically moving house to house?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, sir, what I've been trying to indicate to the Court is that there were times when the Serbian security forces decided that they'd had enough of the nuisance in this particular area and embarked on a very severe operation. Now, whether that was based on intelligence of the KLA from the Vojska Jugoslavije or the MUP, I obviously -- I do not know. But on this particular occasion, they were still completing a -- what we would call a clearance operation to try and make the area as safe as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers or MUP personnel were in the area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I would -- I don't think I've written it in a report. I would guesstimate it was probably, I don't know, a couple of hundred, 300 mixed VJ and MUP with armour support.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: From what I saw on either side of the road and in the villages concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see any civilians in the Rznic area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't expect to. When the Serbs decided to do a clearance operation, then the civilian population usually left the area, obviously for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you go from Rznic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We followed a track towards -- east of the Glodjane area, which came to the -- the concrete sort of open piping that was a water collection system that went into Radonjicka Jezero, the Radonjic Lake, which is on this particular map if that's of any help to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it the canal leading to the lake?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It was like a big monsoon, concrete monsoon ditch, I would think about a 6- or 7-foot deep with concrete, and it was a water collection project that led down to the lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what did you see when you got there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: When we arrived in the area, there were several Serbian security forces around. There were areas that had been taped off like the police put for an accident area. And then -- we were then shown bullet splash marks on the concrete drain area, and there were also, as I think I mentioned in my report, between six and eight bodies, the majority in the water, and I think one or two were on the bank if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the bodies civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: All I can say, sir, is that they appeared to be civilian, they were in civilian clothes, but we did not or were not allowed to physically search these bodies. So they were wearing normal civilian clothing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the state of decomposition of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Again, I think in my report, some bodies appeared to have been there longer than others, bearing in mind the weather was warm and I'm not a qualified coroner. So the bodies certainly looked swollen. How long they'd been there, they could have been there, I think I said in my report, a month and it could have been a few days. It was impossible to tell the distance we were from the bodies themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the MUP say anything to you about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think they -- they indicated that this was a possible or a massacre site, in their terminology. And my comment to the MUP commander was that until all the autopsies are done and until the relevant data is made clear, then I certainly can't report this as a massacre site because we don't know who the bodies are and who's done what to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did you stay there for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think it was about 45 minutes, sir, and during that time I picked up some ammunition that was of Chinese origin that could indicate - and I repeat could - that it was a KLA action.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you find the ammunition in relation to where the bodies were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The ammunition was on the southern or the western side of the -- of this concrete canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "ammunition"? What did you find?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We spent -- we found several spent cases, fired cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I picked them up and I then returned them to the United Kingdom for forensic assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the assessment as to their origin?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think their -- I think, I can't remember now, it was that it -- the ammunition had come from Albania, which was of no great surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I interrupt. First, also, you said you picked up some Chinese ammunition that could indicate that it was a KLA action. On what basis would you conclude from the Chinese if it was Chinese ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was understood, sir, that the KLA had ammunition of Chinese origin. That was just one of the intelligence assessments that had been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, I stress the point, I am not an ammunition specialist, and the autopsy on the ammunition I cannot actually recall seeing but it may be in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why do you say it was Chinese ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Because I think it had Chinese characters on it, which is not unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to have a look at a video, and I'm going to play video 65 ter number 864 from the beginning. I'm playing it without the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just pause the video at 1.52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is this being tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P72, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to be clear that Mr. Re is not going to stop the film at this point, because the witness hasn't been shown any part of the concrete section of the canal and the evidence he's given is that he saw six to eight bodies in the water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am stopping it to ask him about what he actually saw. My question is did he see what's depicted there, and I know what the answer is going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the entirety --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The entirety of what we've seen thus far does not deal with the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I'm also asking myself how you would link it to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll let it play for a bit longer then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Whilst it's playing, if it's of any assistance to Mr. Re and to Your Honours, two things: First of all, I've mentioned this before. There is evidence that the date stamp on that is in error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And secondly, the passage -- I think we're just moving to it now, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, you gave evidence -- it's still playing. You gave evidence some moments ago that you saw you said between six and eight bodies, the majority were in the water and I think one or two were on the bank, if I remember correctly. That was your evidence. What can you say about the video where we are at the moment, which is at 5.32, in relation to your observations of what you saw on the day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The first point that Mr. Emmerson raised is that the date is not correct; and the second is the time is not correct. We were there I think I'm right in saying at 4.00 to 5.00 in the afternoon so --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the point I was making wasn't that this wasn't the date of Colonel Crosland's visit. The point I was making was that the date that's shown on this video has been established not to be the correct date on which the video was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That is clear. We have to discuss that in the case, but I think the gist of the question is now if this is what you yourself also experienced during your visit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of those bodies I remember, sir. As I say, the date, the time, 2.38 a.m., is in the middle of the morning, very early morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that may account for the difference in the number of bodies there that they may have found after our initial visit to the site, which, as I said, I think lasted for about 45 minutes, during which time I recall seeing about six to eight bodies. We haven't yet seen the splash marks on the concrete -- sorry. I beg your pardon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're leaping ahead for the moment. I'm just asking you about the bodies and what you see there, how it accords with your recollection and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These bodies seem well decomposed. So whether they are extra bodies that had been found afterwards, I don't know. But some of the bodies were decomposed; some were not so decomposed as some of the pictures on here, and I suspect the cameraman has gone for the nastier looking bodies. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the bodies in the water, like there's two -- I've paused it at 6.39 on the video.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing those two bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think I recall seeing a couple in this area and then a further one or two where the water is flowing towards the lake were then in the lower segment. You can just see it there. These are quite severe drops, I mean 6, 8, 10 feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We're looking at 6.50. He just -- 6.50 on the video. There's the drops in the canal, the cascades. Is that the section you're talking about below the cascades?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Please do not lead in the -- the question that you've just asked is a knowingly leading question. Please ask the witness where the other bodies that he saw in the water are on that photograph if he can see the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, this is upheld.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if I can recall, Your Honour, gentlemen, ladies, where you see people stood on the bank in the top right-hand corner of your picture was a place from which we viewed the scene. I think there was a body in the last casement down before it goes into the stream, and I think I recall one further body down or upstream, whichever way you -- downstream, whichever way you like in the stream itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we be clear just in that last answer whether that is nearer to the camera or further away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Further away, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we just for purposes of the record to make sure that we're very clear about this, because I don't believe we're going to be marking this. As I am looking at the video at 6.50.2, there seem to be a total of four separate individuals on the right-hand side of the photograph, two are up on the bank and then there seem to be two individuals standing on the concrete cascade wall. If I understood Colonel Crosland's testimony correctly, he was referring to the two individuals who were in the upper right-hand portion of the photograph, one of whom apparently seems to be holding some form of bag. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, sir, that's correct. There were, I don't know, 20, 30 MUP security force personnel in the area carrying out, I presume, forensic activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Mr. Guy-Smith asking questions for me and I was about to ask about the people there and how it accorded with your recollection of MUP activity in that area when you visited.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I said, sir, the operation was clearly still ongoing when the Serb security force had found this site, I don't recall them saying. And as you can see from the countryside, it is fairly thick vegetation, and there was obviously concerns about security, not just for themselves but also for ourselves as well. As I say, the situation was ongoing and I don't -- wouldn't know whether the Serbs had just arrived there or had been there for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is that now part of your presentation, that quick motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, we just had a glitch and the tape rewound evidently. We were at 6.50. Could we just go back to 6.50 and move it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see on the canal wall there's some marks there, that's at 6.59.7?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I can, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you -- what did you observe about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: If those are the marks that we were shown, there was definite bullet splashes, bullet marks, on one side of the concrete canal, indicating that rounds had been fired into this wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you talking about the inside or the outside of the canal wall that the Serbs showed you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This was on the inside of the concrete drain. So the water is below these -- if these are the same ones that we were shown, because you'll appreciate the film's a bit cut-and-pasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Based on your 37 years of experience with ammunition, weapons, military experience, what was your view of what sort of weapon could have caused those marks on the wall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think some of the areas indicated perhaps a burst of automatic fire had been fired, and others might be single shots. I think they were, if I can remember rightly, they were -- and from the distance we saw them, they were very distinct bullet marks in the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is your -- what did your observations lead you to believe the distance from which those weapons would have been fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, if we had picked -- I had picked up the casings on the bank that we were on, which is the southern or western bank, the range was about between 10 and 15, 20 metres, yeah, about half the way across the current courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you pick up the casings from in relation to those marks which were shown on the video at 7.0?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, sir, it was just on the bank approximately opposite where the bullet strikes were. I say "approximately." I can't remember, under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were those casings consistent with the bullet strikes you observed on the inside wall of the canal, based upon --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- your vast years of experience --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- in the military?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I can't make that professional judgement, sir, because I'm not a qualified armourer. They are indicative of the bullet strikes that I have seen over my service and from the range that they may well have been fired at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Re, that answer clearly shows that the question was a little bit too far going, wasn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was appropriately guided by the answer and the look on Your Honour's face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just take it back just a fraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At 7.26 you can see what looks to be two bodies at the top of the cascades. Again, is that consistent with what you saw when you went there on the 8th of September, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry. I don't think there's any evidence as to what those black items in the water are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- what's the sense of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I won't push that. It may look to me like bodies but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, it is indeed a little unclear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just stop it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- are they the splash marks that you were referring to before in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Keep moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just stop there at -- just go back a fraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At 8.18 you can see what appears to be the body of a person lying face-down on the outside wall of the canal. Do you recall from when you went there whether that body was in -- was there or not, whether that was one of the bodies that you said you saw lying face-down on the -- or lying on the bank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In all honesty, Your Honour, I couldn't say that that specific body was there. If you look in that area, it's quite a damp area, there's scratch marks and so on and so forth. It may have been uncovered, it may have been the body we saw there. I can't truthfully say that is the body we saw in that position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just stopping there at 8.49, we're looking at the outside wall of the canal and what appears to be holes in it. Do you recall seeing or being shown those particular marks when you went there with the MUP on the 8th of September, 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I think they mainly concentrated on the bigger or the more numerous bullet marks, splash marks on the other side of the canal. I don't recall those being particularly pointed out, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just pause it there. We're at 9.22 there now and it's showing us the part of the -- where the canal ends and the natural ravine or stream goes to the lake. Did you actually go into that area or how far did you stop -- sorry, how far did you go before you stopped?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, sir, we were to the right of where the current writing 248 on the bank there. We could look down into the gully, and as you can see, there's a fair amount of rubbish and detritus in the water itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Amongst the rubbish and detritus, did you see any vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think there was a remains of a car or something. There was something metal. What exactly it was I don't know, which is down in the bottom left-hand corner now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the clip, and for the record I've played from 00 to 9.40. I'm finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: As you are tendering this, what did we see here? Do you have any -- can give you -- can give us any indication about the exact origin and date?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a video, our evidence is, taken by the Serbian MUP on the 8th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This was, as far as the date is concerned, inserted, but apparently there was a mistake in the insert because that couldn't have been 2.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The date's clearly incorrect and there's no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So the date itself is not very --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, but there will be evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- official, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There will be evidence later in the trial from Serbian MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will marked for identification now under the number it has already received. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your testimony in Limaj, which has been tendered in this court, you were referred to or shown a number of what are called DipTels. Can you just very briefly explain to the Trial Chamber for the purpose of these proceedings what DipTels are and what your part was in writing these DipTels.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- there are two types of telegrams sent from an area such as this. One is a diplomatic telegram, DipTel for short, that is usually initiated by the ambassador or the deputy head of mission and, where appropriate, will have military comment inserted by myself. I would initiate what is called a military telegram from the Brit Mil Rep Belgrade, which majority of the time was written by myself, having been cleared by either the ambassador or the deputy head of mission. Now, because I was down in Kosovo for extended periods, four, five, six days at a time, some of these telegrams are signed by the ambassador Sir Brian Donnelly on my behalf because I was not physically able to sign them, but those are the two sources of telegrams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So you mean you would transmit the text from where you were, in the province of Kosovo, and it would be then sent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had a secure set-up that I could either report directly to Belgrade if the incident was serious and the ambassador needed to know about it and I could also telephone direct to Ministry of Defence in London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there a difference between a sitrep or DipTel sent by the ambassador and signed as Donnelly and a telegram sent by yourself from the Brit Mil Rep, British Military Representative, or the DA, the Defence Attache in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I said, sir, the Brit Mil Rep telegrams were based on my reports which were carried out verbally on the spot in Kosovo into a dictating machine and then transcribed once I returned to Belgrade. However, if the incident was serious enough, as I think this was, then I would inform directly through my secure phone both the embassy in Belgrade and also London and any other friendly NATO country who happened to be with me as a matter of urgency that their -- their nations understood the changing situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it fair to describe these documents as contemporaneous reports of the security situation in Kosovo based upon your observations and information available to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's exactly what they are. They are the reports made at the time into a Dictaphone and then transcribed back in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: There are some -- sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. Go on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: There are some gaps in the telegrams because some of the reports were sent directly back to London as a matter of urgency and therefor there may well be gaps in the 70 telegrams that I sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just for clarity, on page 64, line 1, it's -- you said sitrep or DipTel. I think the word "sitrep," you haven't yet explained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Sitrep is military for situation report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- i.e., what was going on at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a binder of documents, and I'm directing your attention to a particular portion which is I can call the non-Limaj telegrams, that is, diplomatic telegrams not tendered in the Limaj case. And I want you to look at the index and I want you to look through those documents, which each of them has a -- a divider in them. I just want you to go through them one by one relatively quickly and just identify to yourself that is, in fact, what those are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we make clear, Mr. Re, we are now holding this binder in our hands, containing so-called non-Limaj telegrams. But here there is a division between non-diplomatic telegrams and diplomatic telegrams, isn't it? Can you lead us a little more clearly. I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the second one in the bundle or the binder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So it's the second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- headed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- "Crosland DipTel proposed exhibits in chronological order binder index, tab 1, first one 8 March 1998, 65 ter number 827" and thereafter next 42 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first seven are signed by the ambassador, Mr. Donnelly, with input from myself. Number 9 is signed by Mr. Landsman who was the deputy head of mission. Number 10 is back to Mr. Donnelly, as is 11, as is 12, 13, 14, 15, and in paragraph 2 in 15 it says: "My DA has now reached Decani area." So that is the type of input I was giving to these telegrams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe I may ask about the blackened lines, what we should imagine the blackened part would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The blackened parts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- blackened parts --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- as I understand it, Your Honour, is the stuff that has been -- information that has been redacted prior to being produced for your court, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those are redactions the British government has made in allowing the use in these proceedings. The British government has made those redactions themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the one you just referred to for the record is one dated the 27th of April, 1998, and has a 65 ter number of 832, it was number 15 on the list. Go on, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: 16 is also signed by Mr. Donnelly, as is 17, 18, 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- just made but I'm receiving messages from behind that I may not be alone in this. The witness has just made a reference to paragraph 2 in the document behind tab 15, and it may -- in which he said I think it makes a reference to my DA now reaching the Decani area in paragraph 2 of the document behind tab 15. Now, if that's what the witness's document behind tab 15 says, it's not what mine says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Unless it's in front of tab 15, is it? Is it tab 14 that the witness is looking at? Yes, I'm sorry, I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Have I gone the wrong way then?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I think it's tab 14, rather than 15 then. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, it's understood that the document after the grey leaf with a number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But that's easy to mix up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Going then to document 19 is an example of a report based on my reporting to the ambassador because he has signed it for me but it's actually from the Brit Mil Rep Belgrade at the time, so that's an example of what I was informing the Court of before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So the number on the top of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I still -- I seem to be still having a problem. I don't know if it's you, Colonel, or it's me. I don't think I'm looking at all at the same documents the colonel is alluding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, I just was trying to make sure we are all looking at the same document. Can you give us the number on top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number at the top --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: With the R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, this is, at least in my binder after tab 19, second part of that whole binder. This is -- this was my first concern, you remember. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please continue, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20 is signed by Ambassador Donnelly -- or is that 21 ? 21 also, 22, 23 - sorry - 24 you will see is sent from the acting Defence Attache. I was back in England on leave for the wedding of my -- our eldest daughter. So the acting Defence Attache made that report and it is again signed by Ambassador Donnelly. 25 is signed by Mr. Donnelly, as is 26, 27, 28. 29 is back to a Brit Mil Rep, again signed by the ambassador. 30 is Mr. Donnelly, 31 is Mr. Donnelly, 32 is also Mr. Donnelly, as is 33 and 34 and 35 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe can we clarify, Mr. Re, do we have to pay attention to the handwritten three-digit numbers which sometimes are contained in addition to the R0 and so on number? Is there a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. It won't form part of the exhibit as loaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 36 is Mr. Donnelly, 37. 38 is signed by Mr. Landsman, deputy head of mission, as is 39, and 40, 41, and also 42, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm moving for their admission into evidence on the basis that these are DipTels emanating from the former military attache's own hand or his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That application is resisted. I made it absolutely clear earlier on. These documents were provided to us as we entered court this afternoon. I have no objection to Mr. Re, if the time is available to him, seeking to elicit from the witness information arising out of particular documents, but to seek to admit them as stand-alone documents when they are in any event composite documents and whenever they have this witness's sitreps or DipTels have been adduced in the past, they have been adduced by showing him a particular document and inviting him to comment upon the contents and explain them. But simply to seek to adduce en bloc a collection of documentation without explanation beyond the fact that it is identified when this is military material, some of which requires analysis and explanation in our submission is not the appropriate approach. I'm not suggesting that a final decision needs to be taken now because I shall be asking Colonel Crosland some questions about certain of his reports during the course of cross-examination, but I would most certainly resist any en masse attempt to exhibit a collection of unexplained composite documents in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would join in those remarks. I think it is probably at this juncture appropriate to have them marked for identification, and as the course of examination continues, certainly by its conclusion, the Chamber will be in a position to make a determination of what's the appropriate method of dealing with their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sure. If I may look to Mr. Harvey --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Like Homer, I nod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yeah. Would you be fine? I would have in mind we would mark them for identification and decide about admission later, in any case was my intention, which we mark them as 42 different exhibits, as they contain --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, they have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- contents of the second part of this binder as the 65 ter numbers also go?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, that would correspond with the next exhibit numbers from whatever the next one is 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, but these are 42 distinct documents, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Also in order to avoid confusion with the first part of the binder. We have now dealt only with the second part of the binder, tab 1 to 42. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I could briefly respond, I -- I mean, I agree with what Mr. Emmerson is saying. For example, in the Limaj trial Mr. Cayley, the senior trial attorney there, took Colonel Crosland through each of the documents and read on to the record the relevant part and asked him to explain their relevance. For me to do so would probably take a full day of testimony and with the other documents, possibly more. I am basically in the Court's hands in terms of timing and I would dearly love to get the colonel to explain in greater detail how he contributed to these military documents, what they mean, how they work in their context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- and how they relate to other aspects of the case, and if I'm allowed the time to do so I would willingly do so and I don't disagree with what the Defence is saying in terms of the mechanism for tendering them in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. I don't think we need this extensive exercise you pictured now, but may I ask, Mr. Crosland, did you -- have you seen them - this is more a general impression now you can give - before, in principle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You will appreciate I have given quite a few testimonies to the Court. As far as I'm aware, I have seen all those documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you explain to us was that -- was how you contributed to most of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I said to the Court that very often I would communicate with the ambassador back in Belgrade or when he was down in Pristina, and inform him of the current and local situation so that he had and also my own Ministry of Defence had the up-to-date situation that was pertinent in Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would suggest we consider this sufficient elucidation for the moment to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I've got no difficulty with that at all but may I make just one matter absolutely clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It is for me at some point today or tomorrow to cross-examine this witness. In the absence of the Prosecution identifying which of these particular documents it seeks to rely upon as evidence against my client and to seek testimony explaining the relevance of the document, I have no notice of the case I have to meet in respect to any one of these documents and so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the difficulty I have is that it's not simply a matter of procedurally how convenient it is to tender, nor is it me, if I may say so, standing on form in this matter; it's a question of substance. If there is material in this -- this particular collection of documents on which the Prosecution seeks to rely, it's given no notice to the Defence as to what the relevance of the document is. And if Mr. Re currently proposes simply to leave it at that, we are not in a position to know what it is we have to cross-examine upon. That being the case, I don't want anybody to be under the misapprehension that by marking it for identification and the witness having identified himself as recognising and being a part author to this document that there could come a situation in which I could concede that it would be fair to admit them because it plainly would be unfair if the Defence were put into a position of cross-examining on them without their significance having been dealt with by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: The situation of course is the same for the members of the Court. We have this material this morning, so we have had no possibility at all to look into what is the content of these binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I'm sure, Mr. Re, you would be able to filter it as to the relevance and as to the point what you would consider exactly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, but we have selected these on the basis of their relevance to the case of there being an armed conflict between the KLA and Serb forces; namely, the MUP and the VJ, during the relevant period of the -- relevant indictment period. I mean, the first one starts on the 8th of March, 1998, summary says: "Parts of Drenica still inaccessible. No evidence of large-scale exchanges at present. The substantial police forces in the area may be moving from Prekaz, scene of the heaviest fighting so far and several other villages," and so on. So every document when you look at them shows the state of security in Kosovo and in particular, relevant to this particular area during the indictment period. That's why we're leading them. And when combined with the material tendered in Limaj you put the two together and you get a picture of the jurisdictional issue -- threshold of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's helpful for Mr. Re to have said on his feet just now for the first time what it is he wants the material for, but it's of very little use to the Defence to have that kind of indication given extempore in court with no notice or notification and no attempt to use the material in the course of evidence in chief and it doesn't affect the position that I outlined to Your Honour a moment ago at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I understand. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, we are coming to the time to make a break anyway, but I would like to suggest, Mr. Re, you could think about it during the break, if you could, having a little more time now beyond your original time budget, give us an idea to what kind of information contained in these documents you are referring. After the break you would be suggested to go through two or three of these documents in a representative way with the witness to show the Defence -- to put the Defence on notice, yeah, what your intention is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- see what they contain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon? The last sentence was not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You mean a sample of what they contain -- a representative sample, I think is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- what we say here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Court adjourns or takes a break now until quarter past 6.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Before we start again, may I ask Madam Registrar, do we already have numbers for these 42 documents being marked for identification or --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. These 42 tabs would be in numerical order. Tab number 1, 70 -- Exhibit Number 73 up to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, sorry P73 up to Exhibit Number P114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. These are marked for identification. Please, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Should we put them under seal? Is there a -- yes. We can later decide if we would lift that seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We're offering them pursuant to Rule 70. They are the restrictions the British government has placed on our using them in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, I want to take you to some of the documents which are in that document range. The first one I would take you to is behind tab -- behind tab 11. 16th of March is what I -- it should be tab 3. And it's a DipTel dated the -- I'm sorry, 9th of March, 19 -- sorry. What am I talking about? 16th -- sorry, 16th of March -- I was reading it the wrong way. 16th of March, 1998. And it's Donnelly written on the bottom of it. And the summary says: "Serbian government invites Kosovo Albanian political parties to talk for the third time," et cetera, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Re, may I now ask you, as you referred to some restrictions the British government has placed on our using these documents in these proceedings, would that mean we would have to go to private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no. We're using them in the same way that we used them in the Limaj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I haven't been to the Limaj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened in Limaj was the Prosecution read the relevant parts on to the record. The British government doesn't want the documents themselves publicly revealed, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, now I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But it's not a difficulty with some of the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think I read that, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I want to take you to -- Colonel, do you have that there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The relevant part is "security situation" and the second paragraph there is paragraph 8, it said: "The Serbian interior ministry said on 14th of March that the 'terrorists' had resumed operations in Kosovo. The statement says the two attacks were carried out on Catholic Albanians in Djakovica, south of Pristina and the Drenica area over the weekend. Two Albanians were wounded. Nobody has been apprehended and LDK says that an Albanian man was shot dead by police snipers on the 14th of March in Srbica, Drenica, this has not yet been confirmed by other sources." The relevant portion I'm asking you about is about the two attacks carried out on Catholic Albanians over the weekend. Now, in the context of your evidence and your monitoring of activities on the ground, can you tell the Court about the significance of what you've written there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: So there seems to be a misunderstanding. I have not written these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I'm under oath to say what I have written and what I haven't written. So I apologise for putting you in a difficult situation, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. I'm not -- I'm not in a difficult position. These are DipTels emanating from the ambassador, under the hand of the ambassador. I'm asking you about -- when I said you wrote, that was my error.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the significance of that particular passage.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We were briefed at reasonably regular intervals by the Vojska Jugoslavije, because as I said we are -- I am only accredited to the Vojska Jugoslavije. And they would indicate at these briefings that the very poorest nature of the Albanian and Macedonian border was heralding further incursions and incidents within what was the province of Kosovo which was then sovereign territory of former Yugoslavia. And therefore, every event that was assigned to, let's put it, Albanian activity would be mentioned as part of their ongoing information programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The source of the information there are you saying was the Serbian military?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one I take you to is behind tab 6, the 24th of March, 1998. I take you to paragraph 2 where it says: "The 9th of March Contact Group statement requires the following of the FRY: Withdraw special unit -- police units and cease action by the security forces affecting the civilian population." Paragraph 3 says: "My DA," and I assume that's Defence Attache, that is you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Reports that a substantial police presence meaning 100 to 200 APCs check-points remains in the Drenica area. Their positions are still being reinforced, given the impression they intend to stay for the foreseeable future. Special forces in Decani and Djakovica are at a high alert level and reliable reports are coming in of renewed fighting in this region and two others. We shall report on these separately once the picture is clear." I want you to comment on the source of the information if you still can which you have given to Mr. Donnelly to report on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That, sir, would be based on a report -- a tour of mine in the area of Kosovo which included going around the Drenica, which as I've indicated there still had a very heavy Serbian security presence, which is understandable, bearing in mind we're only two weeks from the initial Donji Prekaz problems. The special forces in Decani and Djakovica, we found those out by visiting that area and an artillery position at Decani by physically going -- driving through it. And So the implications that special forces were involved, again, makes good military sense but also indicates that the situation was beginning to get or had more serious connotations to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that what's -- is that what you mean by saying they were on high alert?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the difference between the special forces and the regular MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Special forces are used on high-value targets, they're also used to gather intelligence, and they have systems and intelligence systems that the normal troops do not have, and bearing in mind we -- or they were trying to get information primarily adjacent to the Albanian border with Kosovo because this was, as I've said before, was where the perceived resupply of men and materiels would be coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the special forces part of the MUP or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The special forces are Vojska Jugoslavije. The MUP had their own special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It says: "Reliable reports are coming in of renewed fighting in this region and two others." Just concentrating on this region, can you now say what the reports were of the renewed fighting in that region?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think that would refer to probably the area around Junik and the -- generally the western area of Kosovo, Decani being a major headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next I want to take you to is headed: "Incident at Babaloc" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon, can we also hear -- check the sources of information. It wasn't actually quite clear to me in the first example when you asked for that and in page 78, line 11, the answer then was -- or actually, your question was: "The source of information there, are you saying was the Serbian military?" And the answer was: "That's correct, sir, yes." And --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- I'm not so sure if that is sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to draw Your Honours' attention and Mr. Re's attention to the date of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. That's the second --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- apparent significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- question. Yes. Can we discuss the date also.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to clear up His Honour Judge Hoepfel's question there, Colonel, in relation to the source of information being the Serbian military, can you expand a bit on what your sources were within the Serbian military which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Actually there for --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- for that, we would have to go back to the tab 3 because there was a question to tab 3 and then jump again to tab 6. Sorry for that complication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, I could help with a few words if I'm allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what is attempted to be said here by number 3 is that on paragraph 4: "My Defence Attache has been touring in Kosovo today," and then goes on to say: "Drenica is quiet," et cetera. I think what the ambassador is trying to convey to people that at this early stage when little interest was being taken in the problems that were going to accrue within Kosovo, one was trying to put a flavour of the depth and spectrum of operations that were starting to unfold. The initial attack on the Jashari family in Prekaz had probably taught the Kosovo Liberation Army a lesson, as I indicated earlier. We're now looking -- we're attempting to look at a wider picture of what was going on within the province of Kosovo and quite naturally as an ex-special forces officer -- as a special forces officer, one is looking for the indicators that a regime or an army or a security force, whatever you would like to call the Serbian, is preparing to defend its borders. As I indicate here, Kosovo then was a sovereign part of Serbia -- of Yugoslavia. And therefore the border incursions were taken extremely seriously by the Vojska Jugoslavije and the MUP and they were preparing, in my humble opinion, correctly and carefully to try and prevent the border becoming a very open sieve as it did later on in March 1998. I hope that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So can we say that VJ and MUP together provided information you needed for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. The Vojska Jugoslavije had border security as their primary task in the early days, and the internal security was actually that of the MUP. It then merged as the situation became more serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you for making it more precise. Now we can go back again to tab 6. Please, I can hand over to you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware or given information about an attack by Serbian MUP military forces on the Haradinaj family compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not -- not at this stage, no, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe we can address the date, as Mr. Emmerson proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was on the 24th of March, 1998. Does that assist your memory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we get an explanation how we can read the date, I mean for the Bench it's clear, but maybe it's a precision necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry -- the method of reading the date I think is clear. The first figure is the day of the month. My understanding is that the following four figures are a time, and then the month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The significance is simply, as Mr. Re points out, the 24th of March was the day of the attack on Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Of course. That's quite an -- quite a relevant date. It's clear to us. And can you -- do you want to have this confirmed, that this is the date, or what was the gist of your question -- which is a remark, I have the impression?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm entirely happy. Maybe for the sake of the record Mr. Re want to confirm that the method of reading the date as I've suggested is correct, i.e., the first two digits are the date and then the second remaining digits are the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is what I was meaning also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's quite correct, but time probably doesn't allow me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think it would be the witness to clarify that or would you like to explain this or better to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is what Mr. Emmerson and with my agreement correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The date appears and then the time, and Zulu is the time zone that we were working in, which is one hour ahead of Greenwich Mean Time. What perhaps is further clouding the issue is that these reports were sent at the time/date stated but sometimes -- many times refer to events that have already gone through and may be linked to events going ahead, so there is a plethora of times that confuse the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And time doesn't probably permit me, but in the Limaj testimony Exhibit 92 -- 92, tab 5 which is tab 4 of the Limaj P92 exhibits is -- does refer to that particular exhibit. It's in the evidence in the Limaj transcript. If I could take you to the next one, which is Kosovo incident at Babaloc. The date is the 22nd of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the tab number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The tab would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tab 12 it's headed: "Kosovo: Incident at Babaloc" and "Summary: FRY warned of concern at reported Yugoslav Army involvement in fighting around Babaloc on 22nd of April. Deny any change of policy." And: "Detail," at paragraph 2, "Telecons under reference discussed media reports of fighting around Babaloc (in the Decani region, halfway between Pec and Djakovica, about 15 kilometers from the Albanian border) in which the Yugoslav Army was said to have been -- or said to be involved, and our grounds for considering them credible. It was agreed that I should immediately warn the FRY of our concern. Paragraph 5 refers to: "Tension is particularly high because the Serb refugees from other villages in the Decani region have taken temporary refuge in a disused recreation camp near Babaloc. Journalists and others visiting the area today came under attack with stones and fists from angry Serbs." It's signed Donnelly. Did you visit the area of Babaloc at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think that I did make a tour into that area because it's, as this report says, and as I have indicated to the Court before that the area between Pec and Djakovica on the border was, again, an area of great concern to both entities. And initially, most of the villages from as far away as Junik north towards Pec were cleared of their inhabitants, whether they be Serb or Albanian. Some of the people landing up in the Rugovska pass and others moving across into either Montenegro or into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the source of information about -- it says: "Telecons and reference discussed media reports of fighting around Babaloc." What was the source of the information about the fighting and the deployment -- or the alleged involvement of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, there is initially a complete denial by the Vojska Jugoslavije that they were at all engaged in operations against the insurgent bands, and this was kept up for a very long time, I think up until about August when Colonel-General Ojdanic eventually admitted that the Vojska Jugoslavije had been involved in operations, despite the fact that I had seen and produced a video which was given to the Vojska Jugoslavije of artillery, main battle tanks, and the major destructive parts -- sorry. And the major destructive parts of the Vojska Jugoslavije being used in counter-insurgency operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm -- what I'm just asking you about at the moment is the source of your information in that specific report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think it probably refers to one of my own reports based on a visit to the area and appreciating what I had seen at first hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you go to the next document, the next tab, the date is the 23rd of April, 1998, and it's headed: "Kosovo security sitrep at 1400Z 23rd of April. Summary 1: Largest and most heavily armed Yugoslav Army VJ presence in Kosovo since the beginning of crisis. Concentrated in border areas but most visible elsewhere. Aircraft and helicopters in use. Gun emplacements in strategic positions, but no reports of major conflict in -- life in bigger towns proceeding normally. One report of two Albanians killed and six to eight injured following attack on VJ patrol this morning. It sounds like -- suspiciously like similar report TUR. Then goes to "Detail." "My DA has now reached the Decani area and has confirmed the essence of the media and other accounts about the situation reported in TUR," T-U-R. Going down: "Orao," O-r-a-o, "('Eagle') jet bomber not normally based in Kosovo has been overflying the Decani area, together with Gazelle helicopters. There are some signs that the MUP and VJ may be working together." Paragraph 3. I'm going through it quickly: "Tensions remain high, but there has not as yet been any major escalation in any of the bigger towns like Pec and Djakovica. Life is proceeding normally." I just want you to comment in general terms, bearing the time we have, about the source of your information, you being the DA who has reached Decani there and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: So this information is based on my visual, factual reporting on the spot from Decani and the other areas mentioned. It makes perfect sense that as the situation was deteriorating, the Serbian security forces were taking what they call appropriate measures to defend their sovereign territory, and these included the various facets that we have talked about in paragraph 2, the fact that a jet bomber called an Orao was seen in the area again indicated the seriousness of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's TUR, T-U-R?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Good point. I think it must refer to another telegram, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: While the witness thinks about this question, I also would have asked that -- can I clarify, Mr. Re, do you have three pages of this document or -- in my binder there's only one page, and then it goes on with three pages later, according to this R04, and so on, number. We should maybe supplement the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have checked that on our system, I did a search, and I couldn't find the second page. I did it before I came to court, but I will make another inquiry. It doesn't seem like we've entered it onto our system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We will check that also with the 65 ter number, so we will be able to find it probably. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you could turn to tab 15, please, Colonel, which is 27th of April, 1998. The summary says: "Reports of three major incidents over the weekend. Three Albanians killed in a gun battle west of Decani early Monday morning. VJ action to prevent 200 Albanians crossing the FRY-Albania border near Prizren and a four-hour fire-fight near Lake Radonjic. Funerals of nine Albanians killed in the 23rd April border incident." "Detail: "Security. "2. There have been reports of three major incidents over the weekend. First, three Albanians were reported dead in a gun-battle with VJ troops west of the town of Decani in the early hours of Monday morning" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: A little slower, please. Just a little slower.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Re please slow down while reading documents, otherwise we are entirely unable to follow at this pace. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The interpreters are saying exactly the same: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "The VJ claim to have stopped 200 Albanians illegally crossing the FRY-Albania border near Prizren on Saturday night/Sunday morning. The Albanians are reported to have left large quantity of weapons and ammunitions behind. The VJ claim to have taken no casualties. There are no reports of Albanian casualties. Four-hour gun," sorry, "fire-fight near Lake Radonjic between Decani and Djakovica on Saturday evening apparently left no casualties." I just want to ask you to comment on that. Was that based upon information that you provided to Mr. Donnelly while you were in Kosovo or does it come from another source?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This would be provided by Vojska Jugoslavije in Belgrade as part of -- as part of their ongoing analysis of a worsening situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have any better information on the four-hour fire-fight near Lake Radonjic between -- on the Saturday evening?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The southern end of Lake Radonjic was a major Serb army MUP base, and therefore a likely target area. I can't confirm or deny whether they -- this particular fire-fight took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say from this who the fire-fight was between?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I suspect it was from a vehicle check-point, an isolated Serbian security pocket that may have been bumped into by the KLA and a lengthy fire-fight took place with, apparently, no casualties, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Which just indicates that a lot of -- you know, both sides fired off an awful lot of rounds into the air and didn't really achieve a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one I want to take you to is the 28th of April, 1998, tab 16, and it refers to in paragraph 3: "Beta, a local independent news agency, is reporting that eight Albanians were killed in police activity against the village of Glodjane near Decani, widely believed to be a KLA headquarters. Two people, apparently Albanians in the process of carrying out an attack, were killed in an incident near a police check-point on the Prizren-Orahovac road." Same question: What is the source of the information there which has gone into this DipTel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As it states, sir, it is from Beta, which is the independent news agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A better question from me would have been: What is the reliability of the source which is quoted there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think that it's a reasonable source. It's indicative of the number of assaults that were being carried out throughout the province of Kosovo during this period. It is impossible for any person to be at each and every incident and to verify those incidents, so that is why you're getting different sources telling of different incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please go to the next one which is behind tab 17, and that's dated the 29th of April, 1998. And under "Security" it says: "The number of incidents reported by the media over the last 24 hours is smaller than in recent days, but my DA," that's you, "who was in Kosovo on the 28th of April assesses that the number of police in the area was higher than at any stage so far in the crisis and that army -- VJ activity is also at its highest level. The risks of a major clash remain very high. One unconfirmed Albanian report claims that four VJ personnel were killed in incidents on the 27th of April." The question I have there is: Where in Kosovo did you go to compile this report and what did you see that led you to report that and what was the -- what was its significance? There's three questions there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it just reinforces what I've just said, sir, that because I was touring down there on a very, very regular basis, one could accurately note, physically note, the positions of most of the Serbian security forces, and you would see whether there had been a change or there had not. There was a lot of propaganda suggesting that all the forces in the province of Kosovo were assigned to 52 Corps, the original army unit based in Kosovo. We had evidence at time that extra units had been put into Kosovo. We also worked out from the very numbers of the MUP that they also were on a higher alert by the amount of men and the vehicles that had registration marks outside of the province of Kosovo. So I think this paragraph here indicates that in my opinion there was still a very major risk and that tensions were extremely high. There was a state of -- you know, not quite war because war is to be declared, but there was a state of combat, if you will, between the Serbian security forces and the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll take you to the next one which is the 8th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's two more I want to take him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's tab 18. And it says paragraph 5, under "Security: "Fighting around Ponosevac continues. My DA was forcibly prevented from entering the area on the 7th of May. This is the first time since the start of the conflict that this has happened. He could hear a fire-fight in the background. DA this morning reported that the current level of VJ activity in Kosovo is probably the highest since its deployment in the Eastern Slavonia two years ago," and then it goes on. Can you just very briefly tell us what that was about.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We were touring in the area and, I think, stayed overnight at Djakovica, and therefore were -- we then attempted to move west of Djakovica towards the border area towards this town called Ponosevac; and that is where we were stopped by the Vojska Jugoslavije, who would not allow us in to a border security area. Perhaps it may help, Your Honour, if I explain that in an operational area, if I was in charge of operations, I would not like Defence Attaches and other people running around my patch seeing what we were doing. So why we were allowed such access I don't know, perhaps it was the whiskey I was carrying. But it's an extraordinary -- and I've said this before, that we did get access to areas that other people did not. But it reinforces the point I tried to make some time ago that the border area, particularly west of the major road, Prizren to Djakovica and up to Pec, was an extremely dangerous and fought-over area for all the reasons I've already given the Court. Ponosevac, again, was about 10 kilometres from the border itself, a VJ/MUP base leading up to Qafe Morina which is a border-post right on the Albanian border and more or less in the heart of where a lot of the resupply was done from Albania. So it was an area of major interest and concern to both sides as to who controlled this area. I hope that clarifies the situation a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The last one in this series I wish to take you to is the 28th of May, 1998, that's behind tab 22.
